approved: Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would cut red tape for businesses covered by the Comcare workers' compensation scheme.
It would let the regulator grant a single self-insurance licence to a group of related companies instead of requiring each to apply separately.
The government says the changes would save the economy $32.8 million each year for the next 10 years.
Introduces a 'national employer' test for corporations to join the Comcare scheme.
Allows the Commission to issue group licences to related companies.
Removes the need for the Minister to declare a corporation eligible for a self-insurance licence.
Extends work health and safety law to new self-insurers.
Excludes compensation for injuries during breaks away from the workplace or caused by serious misconduct.
Australian Government and ACT employees, employees of licensed private corporations, and corporations seeking self-insurance under the Comcare scheme.

Keith Pitt It is my great pleasure to rise to speak in the debate on the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014. Before we got to the details of the bill, we had the unfortunate circumstance of sitting through the contributions from the member for Griffith and the member for Corio last night. I would like to make some comments on the contributions from that side of the chamber. Certainly, the proposition put forward that Comcare simply do not have enough inspectors to enforce this legislation is plain wrong. My understanding is that, effectively, every state has some accreditors and inspectors from the state population who can enforce not only this legislation, but the state legislation and a whole pile of other things—including electrical safety acts and a wide range of legislation, including Comcare legislation. I wonder how those opposite think that this has been done for the last 15 years or more. Quite simply, we have public servants; we have federal activities; we have federal ownership of assets all over this country. Comcare has been providing those services for well over a decade, to the best of my knowledge. So it is quite simply outrageous that opposition members make these claims. I will now turn to the bill itself. This is a bill which effectively allows employers who operate over multiple jurisdictions to insure through one agency, which is Comcare. It is about reducing red tape. As someone who has worked in the industry for many, many years, I know that it is exceptionally difficult for companies to cross state borders and operate across a range of legislation. I will give you some very simple examples. Argued that Labor opposes the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 because it strips injured workers of rights under Comcare, citing the removal of off-site recess break cover expected to save licensees $850,000 a year and warning it introduces a new exclusion for workers who die or are permanently impaired amid alleged wilful misconduct.

Argued that the government supports the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 as a red tape reduction measure implementing the 2013 Hanks review, estimating it will cut regulatory burden for eligible corporations by an average of $35 million a year over the next decade.

Argued in support of the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, saying it would let multistate employers self-insure under a single national Comcare scheme and cut compliance costs, citing Woolworths' estimate that a single national work health and safety system could save about $400000 a year.

Argued against the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, saying it would let more national employers self-insure under the Comcare scheme at the expense of injured workers, noting Comcare has only 44 inspectors nationwide compared with hundreds in state based schemes.

Argued in support of the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill, defending the coalition's December 2013 decision to lift a moratorium on multistate employers self-insuring through Comcare, and said the changes are expected to cut regulatory costs by $33 million a year over the next 10 years.

Argued against the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, saying it would lift a moratorium in place since 2007 on national employers self-insuring through the Comcare scheme, and criticised the minimal test requiring only that a company operate in more than one state.

Argued in support of the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, dismissing Labor's opposition as protecting union access under state schemes, and said Comcare's 44 inspectors would grow in line with new entrants as the reforms streamline multistate employers from up to eight different safety regimes to one.

Opposed the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill, describing a 1996 crane collapse at the Twin Towns Services Club that killed two of his brother's workmates, Rodney Taula Masak and Wayne Master, and warned the bill's Comcare scheme offers fewer benefits than state schemes, capping common law compensation at $110,000.

Supported the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation bill, arguing regulation had become excessive, and cited a 59-year-old Tasmanian fisherman whose 30-year coxswain certificate was no longer accepted, forcing him to complete a refresher course, a first aid certificate and other requirements costing $1,500.

Supported the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, arguing that allowing multi-jurisdictional employers to use Comcare would reduce red tape and costs. Cited accreditation burdens, including federal requirements for projects over $5 million and Queensland prequalification levels 1 to 4, and criticised pass-through costs that could add 30 or 40 per cent.

Argued that the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 would weaken workers' compensation and workplace safety protections, especially for injured workers in manual occupations, and urged the government to guarantee that no worker would be worse off.

Opposed the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, arguing that it would centralise workers' compensation by drawing national employers into Comcare, undermine state responsibilities and safety protections, and burden the scheme's 44 inspectors with wider duties.

Summed up the debate by supporting the bill as a measure to reduce regulatory burdens, expand Comcare access for national employers and exclude some injuries from compensation, announcing projected savings of $32.8 million each year for the next 10 years and rejecting claims that safety would be weakened.
